newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stock drop not seen start of big correction.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stock drop not seen start of big correction.

text.p: A sharp drop in Wall Street stocks Thursday is not the start of a big retracement of the last two years of gains, analysts said, blaming instead an unusual combination of events.

"I don't think this is the beginning of the long-awaited but oft-postponed correction," said William LeFevre, analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum. A correction is usually defined as a 10 percent pullback in stock prices from a peak level.

LeFevre said that, with many players away ahead of a three-day market holiday, there were fewer buyers around to absorb Thursday's selling. He said investors were spooked when falling bond prices pushed the yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury issue to 7.09 percent. Also, many investors were anxious amid questions about the value of an Indonesian gold discovery that propelled a Canadian gold mining stock, Bre-X Minerals Ltd into the stratosphere.
Traders noted that a bond yield over seven percent generally attracts funds from stocks into bonds. The yield has risen from 6.35 percent at the end of 1996.

The latest rise in bonds followed Tuesday's move by the Federal Reserve to raise short term interest rates 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. Major U.S. banks raised their prime rates to 8.50 percent from 8.25 percent.
The decline of 140 points in the Dow industrials to 6741 Thursday, if not a bearish signal, at least represented a flashing caution light to many participants.

"We don't see a big market break as much as we see a lot of sloppy market conditions during the next six months," said Karl Rauch, managing director at Rubicon Asset Managementa, Bala Cynwyd, Pa. He said many stocks are overvalued and vulnerable to disappointments in cash flow and earnings.

Rauch is telling clients, depending on their age and tax situation, to keep 30-40 percent of their portfolios in cash, 20-30 percent in tax-exempt securities and the balance in small and mid-cap equities.

LeFevre said he found it encouraging the Dow retraced about 80 points of its losses in the final 30 minutes on Thursday. He said New York Stock Exchange volume of about 481 million shares, moderately active by recent standards, did not suggest a major run for the exists had begun.
